```{r setup}
library(bibnets)
```

## Why attention weighting

Standard co-occurrence treats every pair in a list as equally related. In a
keyword list, the first and second terms receive the same link weight as the
first and tenth terms; in a collaboration list, adjacent collaborators receive
the same link weight as distant collaborators. This can make long lists produce
dense networks in which close and distant relations are not distinguished.

Attention weighting addresses this by borrowing the principle behind attention
mechanisms in large language models and graph attention networks: attention is
a normalised distribution over the items of a sequence that concentrates on
the positions that matter (López-Pernas et al., 2025). In `bibnets`, each item
of a paper's ordered list receives a positional weight from the chosen
profile, the weights of one list sum to one, and a co-occurrence link receives
the product of its two items' weights. Instead of giving every co-occurring
pair the same weight, attention weighting makes links between highly weighted
positions count more than links between lightly weighted ones. This is most
natural for keyword co-occurrence and collaboration networks where list order
carries information.

Because the weights of one list sum to one, a paper's total link weight is
`(1 - sum(w^2)) / 2`, which stays below one half however long the list is. A
long list therefore adds somewhat more than a short one (0.16 for two authors
under `"lead"`, 0.48 for fifty) but can no longer swamp the network, as it
does under full counting, where fifty authors create 1,225 full-strength
pairs. The weights are a fixed positional rule, not learned content-based
attention, and the profile you choose states the ordering assumption
explicitly.

## The four profiles

`attention` takes one of four profiles. Each shapes how a paper's contribution
is distributed over ordered items, then normalises the result to sum to one.

| Profile | Attention concentrates on | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| `"lead"` | early positions | weight is highest at the first position and falls quadratically down the list |
| `"last"` | late positions | weight rises quadratically toward the final position |
| `"proximity"` | the middle of the list | weight rises linearly from both ends toward the centre (`min(position, n + 1 - position)`), so links among central items are strongest; the weight of a link depends on where its two items sit, not on how far apart they are |
| `"circular"` | both ends of the list | weight is highest at the first and last positions and lower toward the middle |

## A worked example

Three papers, with author order preserved:

```{r data}
papers <- data.frame(
  id      = c("P1", "P2", "P3"),
  authors = c("Alice; Bob; Carol", "Alice; Dave", "Carol; Alice; Eve"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
```

The canonical use case for attention weighting is ordered keyword and
collaboration data, where neighbouring items are expected to be more closely
related than distant items. Byline order is a special case: some fields use it
to encode lead contribution, senior contribution, or both.

With plain full counting every co-authorship link weighs the same per paper,
so the strongest tie is simply the pair that appears together most often:

```{r full}
author_network(papers, counting = "full")
```

Switch to `attention = "lead"` and the weight concentrates on early byline
positions. Alice, who leads two of the three papers, now anchors the strongest
ties:

```{r lead}
author_network(papers, attention = "lead")
```

Switch to `attention = "last"` and the emphasis moves to the final position, so
links involving the last-listed authors rise to the top instead:

```{r last}
author_network(papers, attention = "last")
```

The `count` column is identical across all three — it is the raw number of
shared papers. Only `weight` changes, because attention re-distributes each
paper's credit by the selected ordering rule. The choice of profile can reorder
which collaborations look strongest, so it should match the ordering convention
of the corpus.

## Attention is a deliberate choice, not a default

`attention` and `counting` are mutually exclusive. When `attention` is set, the
network is built directly from positional weights and the `type` and `counting`
arguments are ignored; the result is labelled with the profile, and the
header of the printed edge list shows it, so a saved edge list records the
assumption that produced it:

```{r label}
author_network(papers, attention = "proximity")
```

The header reads `author_attention_proximity` and `counting: proximity`.
Alice sits in the middle of P3 and is one of only two authors on P2, so her
links take the largest share: Alice and Dave, the sole pair of a two-author
paper, top the list.

Leave `attention` unset (the default) to use ordinary counting, where you can
choose `"full"`, `"fractional"`, or one of the position-aware counting methods
instead.

## Where attention applies

Attention is available wherever list order is meaningful: author, keyword,
country, and institution networks.

```{r where, eval = FALSE}
author_network(data, attention = "lead")
keyword_network(data, attention = "proximity")
country_network(data, attention = "circular")
institution_network(data, attention = "last")
```

For keyword, country, and institution networks the "position" is the order in
which the field is listed for each paper. Proximity fits lists whose central
items are the focal ones; `"lead"` fits lists ordered by importance, such as
keywords entered most-important first.

## How it works

For each paper, attention applies the selected ordering rule to the list
positions and normalises the resulting weights to sum to one. These weights
fill the paper's row of the works × entities matrix, and the projection
multiplies them, so a link's weight is the sum, over the papers the two items
share, of the product of their positional weights. Because each paper's
weights sum to one, its total link weight stays below one half, and no single
paper — however many items it lists — can dominate the result.
